reading.document_title: Slabic, A., et al. 2024. Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide, Revision A (NASA/TM-20240011783)
reading.method:
Section 4.0-4.11 ("Picking a Simulant: Figures of Merit"). The document defines a Figure of Merit (FoM) as "an 'algorithm for quantifying a single characteristic of a simulant and provide a clear measure of how well a simulant and reference material compare' (Rickman et al., 2010)." "FoM values are calculated using equations that output a value between 0 (nothing like lunar regolith) and 100 (exactly like lunar regolith)." Originally FoMs were "inner products" between unit vectors for the simulant and the lunar reference point (perfect agreement = unity/100, complete disagreement = zero); updated calculations follow Metzger et al., 2019. Seven properties are scored, each with its own equation and its own lunar reference dataset built from Apollo/Luna returned-sample data:
- Mineralogy (Phi_M) and Chemistry (Phi_E): both use an l1-normed "intersection" (overlap) of composition vectors, Phi = ||S ∩ R||_1 = sum(min(s_i, r_i)) over relevant mineral groups or oxides, comparing the simulant to the AVERAGE MODAL MINERALOGY / BULK OXIDE CHEMISTRY of its assigned lunar region (Highlands, Low-Ti Mare, or High-Ti Mare), aggregated from Apollo XRD data (Taylor et al., 2019) and multiple oxide-chemistry literature sources.
- Particle Size Distribution (Phi_PSD): sum of min(f_i^S, f_i^R) over the 25th/50th/75th weight-percent-passing percentiles (Q25/Q50/Q75), comparing the simulant to its region's averaged Apollo PSD quartiles (Graf, 1993).
- Particle Geometry (Phi_G): average of two linear-scalar-difference terms for root form factor (sqrt(FF)) and aspect ratio (AR), each of form max(0, 1 - (1/w)|S-R|/R) with w = 0.5 (a 50% "off-nominal" threshold), compared against a single bulk-averaged Apollo value (not region-specific) from four Apollo samples (10084, 15601, 64501, 67461).
- Material Density (Phi_D): linear scalar difference max(0,1-(1/w)|rho_S-rho_R|/rho_R) of averaged rho(min)/rho(max) values, w = 0.5, against aggregated Apollo/Luna sample density data.
- Shear Strength (Phi_SS): average of two linear-scalar-difference terms for cohesion (C) and angle of internal friction (phi-degree), w = 2.5, against a single reference point obtained by averaging Carrier et al., 1999 cohesion/AoIF values across depth ranges.
- Magnetic Susceptibility (Phi_MS): average of logarithmic scalar differences of MS values (in 1e-9 m3/kg), w = 5, against regional averages of Apollo MS data (Rochette et al., 2010).
All scores share the same 0-100 scale (0 = no similarity, 100 = identical to the lunar reference); simulants lacking sufficient measured data for a property are marked "n/a" in the tables rather than scored. A final Table 24 "Simulant Figure of Merit Summary" chart simply reprints all seven per-property scores together in one grid per simulant; the document does not compute or print any single overall/mean/composite FoM score.

reading.notes:
85 FoM rows extracted, covering 14 simulants across 7 properties. Only rows with an actual printed numeric score are included; every simulant/property cell printed as "n/a" (insufficient data) was omitted per the task rules rather than reported as a score — these are: Mineralogy (CSM-LHT-1, CSM-LMT-1, GreenSpar, OPRH3N, OPRH4W30, OPRL2N), Density (GreenSpar, OPRH4W30), Shear Strength (GreenSpar, NU-LHT-2M, OPRH4W30), Magnetic Susceptibility (OPRH3N, OPRH4W30). All scores independently verified against page-image renders (pp. 32 and 52) to confirm no OCR/text-layer garbling; the "0" vs "06" ambiguity for GreenSpar's magnetic-susceptibility score was resolved by viewing the rendered page image, which prints exactly "06" (this looks like a document typo — GreenSpar's raw MS value in Table 22 is 0.95, not obviously consistent with a FoM score of 6 out of 100 given the equation's logarithmic-difference form — but it is reported verbatim as instructed).

Naming inconsistency in the source document, preserved verbatim: "OB-1(A*)" is the name printed in the Mineralogy (Table 4) and Chemistry (Table 8) tables, while every other property table (11, 14, 17, 20, 23) and the summary chart (Table 24) print the same simulant as "OB-1A". Likewise, the underlying PSD data table (Table 10) labels one row "GreenSpar (250µm)" as the specific tested variant, but the actual FoM score table (Table 11) prints just "GreenSpar" for that same score — I used the name as printed in the FoM score table itself for the "simulant" field in each row (i.e., the primary source of the score), and flag the variant name here rather than fabricating a merge.

Reference-material attribution: The seven dedicated FoM score tables (4, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23) list only Simulant + Score, with no explicit "reference" column. reading.document_title: Lunar Regolith Simulant User's Guide — C.M. Schrader (BAE Systems); D.L. Rickman, C.A. McLemore, and J.C. Fikes (NASA/MSFC), September 2010, NASA/TM—2010–216446
reading.method:
The document scores two of its four "primary" simulant properties (composition, particle size distribution, particle shape, bulk density) with a named FoM algorithm; shape and density FoMs are explicitly not scored. Reference material for all FoM comparisons is a single integrated lunar sample: the averaged subsamples of Apollo 16 core 64001/64002 (a lunar highlands regolith core), chosen to match the polar-highlands outpost architecture.

(1) Composition FoM (Table 3): computed with "FoM v.2" data-entry forms/algorithms, captioned as the "FoM Revision 1 algorithm." It combines particle-type modal analysis (mineral grains, glass, lithic fragments, agglutinates — from QEMSCAN/SEM-EDS point counting, see Table 2) with the one solid-solution mineral chemistry term available for both simulants and the regolith — plagioclase feldspar's molar % anorthite — into one unitless score per simulant, printed as "Simulant" vs. "64001/64002 Reference."

(2) Particle Size Distribution FoM (Table 5): computed with FoM size software v.1.0 (released 2007) / v.2.0 (released 2009). It compares a simulant's particle-by-particle size distribution (binned to match the reference dataset) against three different renormalizations of the 64001/64002 reference data: the full "Bulk Average," the "<1-mm Average" subset (recalculated to 100%), and the "Average to 90 μm" subset (recalculated to 100%, used only for the two dust simulants). A given simulant can carry several PSD scores because it may have been measured by more than one analytical method — section/thin-section image analysis, dry sieving, or laser diffractometry — each producing its own comparison against whichever reference subset(s) applied.

The document never states numeric endpoints for the scale (it does not print "1.0 = perfect match" or "0 = no match"), but frames it qualitatively: §5.4.1 notes that because the reference is ≈32 modal % agglutinates and ≈31 modal % lithic fragments, "simulants that do not approximate these abundances will score a low composition FoM score," implying higher = closer match to the lunar reference, lower = more divergent. All printed scores in the document fall between 0.06 and 0.82.

FoM "Shape and Density" (§3.4) are stated to have only "preliminary definitions... and algorithms and metrics are being developed. These FoMs are not included in this TM." §7 repeats that shape-comparison metrics/parameters have "not yet been completed." Table 6 (shape) gives only raw QEMSCAN weight-percent classifications (very angular → well rounded) per simulant with explicitly "No data in these terms exist for lunar regolith," i.e. no lunar-reference comparison and no numeric FoM score — so it yields no FoM rows.

reading.notes:
Verified against a 150-dpi render of PDF pages 23 (printed p.13, Table 3) and 26 (printed p.16, Table 5) — the pdftotext -layout extraction matched the rendered table images exactly, so no OCR/garbling corrections were needed.

Rows are one per (simulant, property, reference-subset), per the task's instruction, so Table 5's 16 simulant/method rows expand to 31 score rows (skipping every printed "–" cell, which means "not run/not applicable," not a score of zero). Table 3 contributes 8 straightforward rows (one reference: "64001/64002").

Exclusions, and why no rows were reported for them (all confirmed by reading the surrounding text, not inferred):
- Table 6 (particle shape, QEMSCAN weight-% by angularity class) and bulk density: excluded because they are NOT FoM scores against the lunar reference. §3.4 states shape/density FoM algorithms and metrics "are being developed. These FoMs are not included in this TM," and Table 6's own text says "No data in these terms exist for lunar regolith" — i.e., there is no reference-material comparison at all for shape, only a simulant-to-simulant qualitative comparison. Section 7 (Shape) repeats that "the defining of the metrics and parameters for analysis has not yet been completed."
- Table 2 (particle-type modal % and plagioclase An% per simulant) is INPUT data used to calculate the Table 3 composition FoM score, not itself an FoM score, so it is not reported as a row.
- Chenobi has no composition FoM (Table 3) row because the document does not report particle-type modal data for it (per §8, its composition is inferred/analogized from OB-1's anorthosite feedstock rather than measured), but it does have PSD FoM rows (Table 5).
- NU-LHT-2C is mentioned as having PSD data but is explicitly excluded from PSD FoM analysis: "the resolution of NU-LHT-2C PSD data is insufficient for FoM analysis" (§6.4), and it is not in Table 3 either — so it has zero FoM rows despite being discussed in the fit-to-use matrix (Table 7, outside FoM scope).
- The document never gives a numeric definition of the FoM scale's endpoints (no printed "0 = no match, 1 = perfect match" statement); this is disclosed in the `method` field rather than invented.

Simulant-name handling: Table 5 row labels carry a parenthetical analytical method (e.g., "NU-LHT-1M (section image analysis)" vs. "NU-LHT-1M (dry sieve)" vs. "NU-LHT-1M (laser diffractometry)") because the same physical simulant was measured three different ways, each yielding its own FoM score set; these are reported as separate "simulant" strings exactly as the table prints them (not collapsed to a bare "NU-LHT-1M"), consistent with the rule to keep a derivative/qualified name intact rather than attaching its score to a bare base-product row.

Three caveats for downstream use:
(1) The document contradicts itself on the composition algorithm. Table 3's caption says 'FoM Revision 1 algorithm', but sections 3.5 and 5.3 say the composition FoMs were computed with the FoM v.2 algorithm, in Matlab.
(2) The body text of 6.3 calls the third reference subset '<90-mm', which is a typo. The table header reads 'Average to 90 μm' and section 6.3.2.2 says '<90-μm fraction'. Both subsets were recalculated to 100 wt.%.
(3) The scale is never stated. The reader's 'unitless, 0-1 implied' is a fair description.

reading.method: This document never uses the term "Figure of Merit" or "FoM" and never prints a numeric (0-1 or 0-100) score. Its one property-by-property simulant-vs-lunar-soil rating is Table 3 ("Comparison of selected regolith characteristics for each simulant examined in terms of their suitability for testing of oxygen extraction technology," Sec. 7.4, p.24). For each regolith characteristic (Bulk Properties: Chemistry, Mineralogy; Grain Characteristics: Shape, Size Dist.; Agglutinate Characteristics: Glassiness, Shape; plus Implanted Solar Particles, Reactivity, Reflectivity, Nanophase Fe, Magnetic Properties, Emissivity) the authors assign each simulant a qualitative, color-coded match rating by expert judgment (not a computed statistic): Green = "simulant provides a close match to lunar soil in most aspects"; Yellow = "lacking in some aspect(s) but likely still acceptable"; Red = "poor match or no attempt to match"; TBD = not yet determined/measured by the authors; N/A = characteristic not applicable to that simulant (not scored). A separate "Value" column (High/Medium/Low, footnoted) records how important each characteristic is for oxygen-extraction methods generally (from Simulant Working Group 2010, Appendix 6) — it is not a per-simulant score. Because the colors themselves carry no printed text, I read them from a 300-dpi page render (pdftoppm) rather than pdftotext, and I cite the printed legend text as the definition of each color. Sections 7.1-7.2 separately compare Exolith/Off Planet simulants qualitatively (in prose, no scores) to Apollo 16 sample 62231 (highland) and Apollo 15 sample 15041 (mare); Tables 1-2 give raw measured values (aspect ratio, median particle size) side-by-side with lunar data, not match scores, so they are not reported as FoM rows.

reading.document_title: Deitrick, S. R. and Cannon, K. M. — Regolith Simulant Report Cards: A User-Friendly Simulant Certification System (LPSC abstract, Colorado School of Mines / NASA JSC)
reading.document_path: papers/LRS/Deitrick et Cannon - REGOLITH SIMULANT REPORT CARDS A USER FRIENDLY SIMULANT CERTIFICATION.pdf
reading.method: A 2-page LPSC abstract describing a certification system the authors were building (explicitly still in development: "This system is currently being set up to automatically generate PDF report cards... before user testing"). It takes analytical data for six simulant properties — bulk chemistry, modal mineralogy, particle size distribution, particle shape, grain density, and magnetic susceptibility — and gives each a per-property "FoM value." That FoM value is multiplied by a property weight assigned per use case (weights are re-normalized if a property has no data) to give a property score; property scores are summed across the relevant properties to give an overall Use Case Score for each of five use cases (Geotechnical, Particle Bonding, Particle-Surface Interactions, Chemical Processing, Human Health). In the Figure 1 worked table the per-property FoM values and the Use Case Scores are on a 0-1 scale with suitability bands >0.75 "Most Suitable," 0.33-0.75 "Suitable," <0.33 "Less Suitable"; the Figure 2 report-card mock-up shows the same six per-property "Figure of Merit Score" values and the same five Use Case Scores restated on a 0-100 scale (e.g. 0.94 to 0.3265 in Figure 1 correspond exactly to 94 and 33 in Figure 2), with the same three suitability labels. The abstract does not explain, and gives no worked example of, how a per-property FoM value itself is derived from raw analytical data (i.e., what lunar reference material or formula converts a measurement into that 0-1/0-100 number) — it only shows the downstream weighting/summation arithmetic. It cites ISO 10788:2014 and Schrader et al. (2010) NASA/TM-2010-216446 as the prior "Figures of Merit" and fit-to-use systems it is trying to replace.
reading.notes:
Rows are empty because every numeric score in this document belongs to an explicitly fictional, illustrative example, not to any real simulant.

The document is a short (2-page) LPSC conference abstract about a certification-system design that the authors say is still being built ("the designs are being finalized before user testing... In the future we will produce a set of report cards for the most commonly used lunar simulants today" — p.1/2, Future Work). It contains no measured/real FoM data for any actual product.

Both tables of numbers trace to one and the same made-up example, named "CRH-1":
- Figure 1 (p.1), captioned verbatim: "Figure 1. Weighing system using example values for FoMs and property weights to calculate use case scores." Its "Property FoM per Use Case" table gives FoM values 0.7 (Chemistry), 0.94 (Mineralogy), 0.2 (Particle Shape), 0.49 (Particle Size Distribution), 0.3 (Particle Density), 0.04 (Magnetic susceptibility) — the caption itself calls these "example values."
- Figure 2 (p.2), captioned verbatim: "Figure 2. Example of a regolith simulant report card main page. For the imaginary simulant CRH-1, it is clear that the simulant is most suitable for use in chemical processing tests." Its report-card mock-up lists "Figure of Merit Score": Mineralogy 94, Chemistry 70, Particle Size Distribution 49, Particle Shape 20, Grain Density 30, Magnetic Susceptibility 4, and Use Case Scores Geotechnical 33, Particle Bonding 53, Particle-Surface Interactions 46, Chemical Processing 82, Human Health 55.

The Figure 2 numbers are simply the Figure 1 numbers rescaled ×100 (e.g. Mineralogy 0.94→94, Geotechnical use-case score 0.3265→33, Chemical Processing 0.82→82), confirming both figures depict the same single hypothetical demo, not two different real simulants. The authors state outright that "CRH-1" is imaginary, and no lunar reference material (sample, site average, or named reference soil) is ever identified as the thing these example values were scored against — the abstract only demonstrates the weighting/summation mechanics of the future system.

Per the task rule ("If the document describes FoM but gives no scores for named simulants, return rows [] and say so in notes"), no row was created for CRH-1 or any other name, since CRH-1 is not a real simulant and publishing its numbers on a public database page would misrepresent an authors'-own-labeled fictional placeholder as a real certified score.

Extraction method: pdftotext -layout was run on the full 2-page PDF (all FoM-relevant text captured cleanly; grep -n -i -E "figure.of.merit|FoM" located every mention). Because the actual score tables (Figures 1 and 2) are graphics/embedded tables, both pages were also rendered with pdftoppm -r 200 and read as images to confirm every numeric value and both figure captions verbatim.
